title: The shape of returns
objectives: Draw a histogram of returns with chosen bins
Overlay a fitted normal curve on a density histogram and read the fat tails

screens.title: Counting by size
screens.prose: Twelve daily returns of an index fund, in %. Forget the order for a moment. We want to know how often each size of move happens.
screens.question: Tap every return from −1% up to, but not including, 0%.

hints.text: A return in this range is negative but no lower than −1%.
There are five negative returns. One of them is below −1%.
−0.85, −0.12, −0.38 and −0.57 are in. −1.04 is below −1%, and −2.47 further still.

feedback.correct: Four of the twelve returns land between −1% and 0%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep returns at or above −1% and below 0%.

byKey.r8c1: −1.04% is below −1%, so it belongs to the next range down.
byKey.r7c1: 0.05% is above zero, so it is in the next range up.

explain.text: You kept the four returns in $[-1\%, 0\%)$. Doing the same for every 1% range gives counts 1, 1, 4, 5 and 1 from −3% up to 2%. Drawn as bars, those counts show the shape of the returns.

screens.title: A thousand days
screens.prose: This simulator draws daily returns from a model of an index fund, with a standard deviation of 1%. Each bar is the share of days in a 0.5% range. The dashed marks are what a normal curve with the same sd would give.
screens.question: After about 1,000 days, roughly what share of days moved less than 1% either way?

options.text: About three quarters
About a half
options.why: Add the four middle bars, from −1% to 1%. Each of the two central ones alone is near a quarter.

options.text: About 95%
options.why: That is the share within 2 sd of a normal. Here 1% is only 1 sd.

options.text: About a quarter: days spread evenly
options.why: You may have judged from a 10-day run. With more days the bars pile up in the middle.

feedback.generic: Add up the bars between −1% and 1% after a long run.

explain.text: The four middle bars hold about three quarters of the days; the model's exact share is 77.0%. The normal marks give 68.3%. A chart that counts values by range like this is a **histogram**.

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw off-screen: the tests read the Axes
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def hist_returns(rets):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    edges = [-0.03, -0.02, -0.01, 0.0, 0.01, 0.02]
    ax.hist(rets, bins=edges)
    return ax

Pass the edges list as `bins`, so the bins match the chart.
`ax.hist(rets, bins=edges)`.

feedback.correct: Five bins, counted the same way you did by hand.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check that you pass the edges as `bins`.

byKey.test-1: There should be five bars, one per pair of edges. Pass `bins=edges`; with no bins matplotlib makes ten of its own.
byKey.test-3: A return on an edge belongs to the bin on its right, and 0.02 belongs to the last bin. `ax.hist` does this for you with `bins=edges`.

explain.text: `bins=edges` fixes the bins, so the counts match the hand count: 1, 1, 4, 5, 1. Test 3 has returns sitting exactly on edges: −0.01 goes to the bin to its right, and 0.02 stays in the last bin. A return outside every edge is silently left out.

screens.title: What the normal promises
screens.prose: A normal curve puts 99.73% of its weight within 3 sd of the mean. A year has about 252 trading days, so ten years have 2,520.
screens.question: In 2,520 trading days, how many days does the normal curve expect beyond 3 sd, either side?

hints.text: What share of days lies outside the shaded band?
Outside is $1 - 0.9973 = 0.0027$, split between both tails.

feedback.correct: About 7 days in ten years, or one every 18 months.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the share outside the band by 2,520.

byKey.one-tail: That is one tail. The question counts falls and rises beyond 3 sd.
byKey.two-sd: That uses 5%, the share beyond 2 sd. Beyond 3 sd it is 0.27%.
byKey.inside: That counts the days inside the band. We want the days outside it.

explain.text: The normal curve leaves 0.27% of days outside $\pm 3$ sd, so $2520 \times 0.0027 = 6.8$ days. The model on the explore screen expects 33.4: its tails hold 1.32% of days. Real index returns sit close to that model.

screens.title: Bars against the curve
screens.prose: Here is the model's exact share of days per 0.5 sd bin. The dashed marks are the normal with the same sd.

state.caption: Beyond ±3 sd: 1.32% of days here, 0.27% for the normal

screens.question: Which statement does the histogram support?

options.text: More days near zero and beyond 3 sd than the normal; fewer in between.
The returns are normal; the gaps are noise.
options.why: These are exact model shares, not a sample, so nothing here is noise. The centre bars beat the marks by a quarter.

options.text: The tails are thinner than the normal.
options.why: You looked at 1 to 2.5 sd, where the bars are lower. Beyond 3 sd they are higher: 1.32% against 0.27%.

options.text: The returns have a lower mean than the normal.
options.why: The bars are symmetric about zero, like the marks. The difference is in the shape, not the centre.

hints.text: Compare each bar with its dashed mark: above or below?
Look at the two middle bars, then at the bars from 1.5 to 2.5 sd.
Middle bars are above their marks, shoulder bars below, and the caption gives the tails.

feedback.correct: A tall peak, thin shoulders and fat tails.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each bar with its mark, in the middle, the shoulders and the tails.

byKey.thin: You looked at the shoulders. Beyond 3 sd the bars beat the normal: 1.32% of days against 0.27%.

explain.text: The centre bars are about a quarter taller than the marks, and the shoulders are lower. Beyond 3 sd the model has five times the normal's share. Returns like this have **fat tails**, and a histogram against a normal curve is how you show them.

screens.title: The curve on the floor
screens.prose: A colleague runs `ax.hist(rets, bins=16)` on 2,520 daily returns with sd 0.01, then plots the normal pdf over it. The dashed marks show the curve's height at each bin. It hugs the floor.

state.caption: Bars: days per bin. Marks: the normal pdf.

screens.question: Why does the curve sit so far below the bars?

options.text: The bars count days; the pdf is a density. `density=True` rescales the bars to area 1.
Returns are not normal, so the curve cannot fit.
options.why: You blamed the data. Even perfectly normal returns would tower over the curve, because the bars count days.

options.text: The curve must be multiplied by the number of days, 2,520.
options.why: Close, but that overshoots. A bin holds about $N \times \text{width} \times \text{pdf}$ days, so the width, 0.005, is missing.

options.text: The curve was drawn before the bars and hidden.
options.why: Drawing order changes what sits on top, not the heights. The marks are low because of their units.

hints.text: What does one unit on the y axis mean for a bar? And for the pdf?
A bar's height is a count of days. A pdf's height is probability per unit of return.
Dividing each count by $N \times$ bin width, $2520 \times 0.005 = 12.6$, puts the bars in the pdf's units.

feedback.correct: Counts and densities are different units.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a bar's height measures and what the curve's height measures.

byKey.notnormal: You blamed the data. Even perfectly normal returns would tower over the curve, because the bars count days.

explain.text: Each bar is a count, up to 607 days, while the pdf peaks near 40. With `density=True` matplotlib divides each count by $2520 \times 0.005$, so the bars have total area 1 like the curve. Now the two can be compared: the tall middle is the fat-tailed peak.

canvas.caption: After density=True: bars and curve in the same units

screens.title: Bars and curve, same units
screens.prose: The normal pdf is $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\, e^{-(x - \mu)^2 / (2\sigma^2)}$. Draw it over a density histogram, using the returns' own mean and sd.
screens.question: Complete `hist_with_normal(rets)`.

widget.starter:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw off-screen: the tests read the Axes
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def hist_with_normal(rets):
    rets = np.asarray(rets, dtype=float)
    mu, sd = rets.mean(), rets.std()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    # 1. a histogram with 40 bins, scaled so its bars have total area 1
    # 2. the normal pdf with mean mu and sd sd, from mu - 4 sd to mu + 4 sd
    return ax
widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw off-screen: the tests read the Axes
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def hist_with_normal(rets):
    rets = np.asarray(rets, dtype=float)
    mu, sd = rets.mean(), rets.std()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.hist(rets, bins=40, density=True)
    x = np.linspace(mu - 4 * sd, mu + 4 * sd, 201)
    pdf = np.exp(-((x - mu) ** 2) / (2 * sd ** 2)) / (sd * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))
    ax.plot(x, pdf)
    return ax

tests.call: round(sum(p.get_height() * p.get_width() for p in ax.patches), 4)

examples.call: round(sum(p.get_height() * p.get_width() for p in ax.patches), 4)

hints.text: Which argument of `ax.hist` gives total area 1?
`np.linspace(mu - 4 * sd, mu + 4 * sd, 201)` gives the x values for the curve.
`ax.hist(rets, bins=40, density=True)`, then build `pdf` from the formula with `np.exp` and `ax.plot(x, pdf)`.

feedback.correct: A density histogram with its fitted normal on top.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check `density=True`, the formula and the x range.

byKey.test-1: The bars add up to more than area 1, so they are counts. Pass `density=True` to `ax.hist`.
byKey.test-3: The curve's peak should be $\tfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}$. Check the factor in front of `np.exp`.
byKey.test-4: The curve should start 4 sd below the mean: `mu - 4 * sd`.

explain.text: `density=True` makes the bar areas sum to 1, the same as the area under the pdf. The curve uses the sample's own $\mu$ and $\sigma$, so any mismatch is shape, not scale. Here the bars poke above the curve in the middle and the far tails.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
To compare returns with a normal:

```python
ax.hist(rets, bins=40, density=True)
x = np.linspace(mu - 4 * sd, mu + 4 * sd, 201)
ax.plot(x, np.exp(-(x - mu)**2 / (2 * sd**2)) / (sd * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)))
```

A bar's height is $\dfrac{\text{count}}{N \times \text{width}}$, so the bars and the curve both have area 1.
screens.question: A density histogram of 1,000 returns has bins 0.002 wide. One bar is 40 high. How many returns are in it?

options.why: You read the height as a count. With `density=True` it is count over $N \times$ width.
That is the share of returns in the bar. Multiply by 1,000 to get a count.
You divided by the width instead of multiplying: $40 \times 0.002 \times 1000 = 80$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the scaling: count = height × N × width.

explain.text: Height times width is the bar's share of returns, $40 \times 0.002 = 0.08$. Of 1,000 returns that is 80.

screens.prose: A risk committee reviews three years of a fund's daily returns, 750 days. They want the histogram against a fitted normal, with the worst day marked. A mark far out in the tail, where the curve is flat, is the case for fat-tail risk.

widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw off-screen: the tests read the Axes
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def shape_figure(rets):
    rets = np.asarray(rets, dtype=float)
    mu, sd = rets.mean(), rets.std()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.hist(rets, bins=50, density=True)
    x = np.linspace(mu - 4 * sd, mu + 4 * sd, 201)
    ax.plot(x, np.exp(-((x - mu) ** 2) / (2 * sd ** 2)) / (sd * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)))
    ax.axvline(rets.min(), linestyle="--", color="grey")
    return ax

tests.call: round(sum(p.get_height() * p.get_width() for p in ax.patches), 4)

examples.call: round(sum(p.get_height() * p.get_width() for p in ax.patches), 4)

ideas: A histogram counts returns by size: `ax.hist(rets, bins=edges)` draws one bar per bin and drops values outside the edges.
To compare with a normal curve, use `density=True` so the bars have area 1, then plot the pdf with the returns' own mean and sd.
Daily returns have a taller peak and fatter tails than a normal: days beyond 3 sd come several times as often.

formula.name: Normal pdf
formula.note: A density bar is count ÷ (N × bin width).

summary.trap: Plotting a pdf over a count histogram puts the curve on the floor. Use density=True.

quiz.prose: A density histogram of 1,000 daily returns uses bins 0.0025 wide. The tallest bar is 24 high.
quiz.question: How many days are in the tallest bar?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count = height × width × number of returns.

byKey.height: You read the height as a count. With `density=True` multiply by width and by 1,000.
byKey.share: That is the share of days. Multiply by 1,000.

explain.text: Height times width is the bar's share of returns: 0.06. Of 1,000 returns that is 60 days.

quiz.prose: `ax.hist(rets, bins=[-0.02, -0.01, 0.0, 0.01, 0.02])` is drawn. One of the returns is 0.035.
quiz.question: What happens to the 0.035 return?

options.text: It is left out, with no warning.
It is counted in the last bin.
options.why: The last bin stops at 0.02. Values beyond the outer edges are not counted anywhere.

options.text: matplotlib raises an error.
options.why: It does not complain. That is why the edges need to cover every return.

options.text: A new bin is added for it.
options.why: With an edges list the bins are fixed. Only an integer `bins` adapts to the data.

feedback.correct: Values outside the edges vanish silently.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which bin could hold 0.035?

explain.text: Every bin lies inside $[-0.02, 0.02]$, so 0.035 has nowhere to go and is dropped. For returns, the dropped values are often the tail days that matter most.

quiz.prose: Daily index returns are compared with a normal of the same mean and sd.
quiz.question: Which description fits most daily return histograms?

options.text: A taller peak, lower shoulders and fatter tails than the normal
Close to the normal everywhere
options.why: Near the middle it can look close. Beyond 3 sd real returns have several times the normal's share.

options.text: Flatter than the normal, with thin tails
options.why: That is the reverse. Most days are quieter than a normal predicts, and a few are far wilder.

options.text: Shifted left of the normal
options.why: The mean is matched, so there is no shift. The difference is in the shape.

feedback.correct: Fat tails and a tall peak.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about the centre, the shoulders and the tails in turn.

explain.text: With the same sd, a fat-tailed histogram puts more days near zero and beyond 3 sd. To keep the sd equal it must have fewer days in between.

quiz.prose: Five years have about 1,260 trading days. A normal leaves 0.27% of its weight beyond 3 sd either side.
quiz.question: How many days beyond 3 sd does the normal expect in five years?

byKey.one-tail: You halved it. 0.27% already covers both tails.
byKey.pct: You multiplied by 0.27 rather than 0.0027. Turn the percentage into a decimal first.

explain.text: 0.27% is 0.0027 as a decimal, and $1260 \times 0.0027 = 3.4$. Real index returns usually show several times that.
